title: Compare the modern GC algorithms (Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) — pause model, best-fit heap size/workload, and defaults by Java version.
shortTitle: Comparing modern GC algorithms — Serial, Parallel, G1, ZGC, Shenandoah — pause model, best-fit heap/workload, and defaults by Java version

s1_definition.profdef: The JVM offers several garbage collectors that reclaim unused heap memory, and they trade off throughput, pause time, and resource use differently. Serial GC uses a single thread and stops the whole application during collection, best for tiny heaps and single-core environments. Parallel GC, also called the Throughput collector, uses multiple threads for stop-the-world collection to maximize total throughput, best for batch work that tolerates pauses. G1, the Garbage-First collector, divides the heap into regions and does most work concurrently with short, predictable pauses, best for large heaps needing balanced latency and throughput, and it is the default since Java 9. ZGC and Shenandoah are low-latency collectors that do almost all of their work concurrently, keeping pauses in the sub-millisecond to low-millisecond range even on very large multi-gigabyte to terabyte heaps, best when consistent low latency matters more than raw throughput.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine cleaning up the paperwork clutter in National Bank of India's offices. Serial GC is one cleaner who makes everyone stop working while they tidy — fine for a tiny one-room branch. Parallel GC is a whole cleaning crew that still makes everyone pause, but finishes fast, so total work done per day is highest — good for overnight batch processing. G1 cleans one room at a time, mostly while staff keep working, pausing everyone only briefly and predictably. ZGC and Shenandoah are near-invisible cleaners who tidy around staff without ever really stopping them, so even a vast head office never freezes — exactly what you want for a customer-facing trading system where a one-second freeze is unacceptable.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick Serial for tiny heaps, Parallel for throughput batch jobs, G1 for balanced large-heap general use (the modern default), and ZGC or Shenandoah when you need consistently tiny pauses on huge heaps.

sections.s2_technical:
Garbage collection reclaims heap memory occupied by objects no longer reachable. The central tension is that doing this safely can require pausing the application — a stop-the-world pause — and different collectors manage that pause differently. The right choice depends on heap size, how many cores you have, and whether your workload cares more about total throughput or about avoiding latency spikes.

Serial GC uses a single thread and performs a full stop-the-world pause for every collection, in both the young and old generations. Because it does not coordinate multiple threads, it has the lowest overhead and memory footprint, which makes it ideal for small heaps, say up to a couple of hundred megabytes, and for single-processor machines or small containers. Its downside is that pauses grow with heap size, so it is unsuitable for large heaps. It is the default in certain small-footprint situations the JVM detects, such as a single available processor.

Parallel GC, historically the default through Java 8, is the throughput-oriented collector. It still stops the world for collection, but it uses many threads to do that work in parallel, so the pauses are shorter than Serial for the same heap and total throughput is high. It is a good fit for back-end batch processing and analytics where the goal is to process as much data as possible and occasional pauses of a few hundred milliseconds are acceptable. What it does not give you is predictable low latency, because a full old-generation collection can still cause a noticeable stop-the-world pause that scales with heap size.

G1, the Garbage-First collector, became the default in Java 9 and is the modern general-purpose choice. It divides the heap into many equal-sized regions and collects the regions with the most garbage first, hence the name. Most of its marking work runs concurrently with the application, and the collection pauses are incremental and aimed at a pause-time target you can set, often around two hundred milliseconds by default but tunable lower. This gives a strong balance of throughput and predictable, bounded pauses on large heaps, which is why it suits most server applications with heaps from a few gigabytes up to tens of gigabytes. Its pauses are short but not sub-millisecond, and they can grow if the heap is very large or the pause target is very aggressive.

ZGC and Shenandoah are the low-latency collectors, designed so that pause times stay in the sub-millisecond to low-single-digit-millisecond range and, crucially, do not grow with heap size. They achieve this by doing almost all of their work — marking and even relocating live objects — concurrently with the running application, using techniques like load barriers and colored pointers in ZGC and a Brooks-style forwarding pointer in Shenandoah so objects can be moved while the application still runs. ZGC originated at Oracle and scales to very large heaps, from gigabytes up into the terabyte range, becoming production-ready in Java 15. Shenandoah originated at Red Hat with similar goals and timing. Both trade a little throughput and extra CPU and memory overhead for their remarkable pause consistency, so you choose them when consistent low latency is the top priority, such as a low-latency trading engine or a large interactive service where a long pause would be visible to customers.

The default by Java version is a useful anchor. Through Java 8 the default was Parallel GC. From Java 9 onward the default is G1. ZGC and Shenandoah are opt-in with flags; ZGC is enabled with a flag and became non-experimental and production-ready in Java 15, and recent Java versions also offer a generational mode for ZGC that improves efficiency. Serial GC remains the automatic choice in constrained single-core environments. Knowing that G1 is the sensible modern default, and that you only move to ZGC or Shenandoah when measurements show G1's pauses are too long for your latency goals, is exactly the judgement an interviewer wants to hear.

The senior-level nuance is that collector choice must be driven by measured requirements, not fashion. You first define a service-level objective for latency, such as a ninety-ninth-percentile pause under ten milliseconds, then measure the actual pause behaviour under realistic load, and only then decide whether G1 suffices or ZGC is warranted. You also account for the cost: low-latency collectors consume more CPU and memory to achieve their short pauses, so on a throughput-bound batch job they would actually reduce useful work. And you remember that a bigger heap is not automatically better — it can make pauses worse for collectors that must scan more live memory — which is a trap the naive "just raise the maximum heap" instinct falls into.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, three very different workloads run on the JVM, and each needs a different collector chosen deliberately.

Problem 1 — A nightly settlement batch job processes millions of trades and cares only about finishing fast; a few pauses are irrelevant because no customer is waiting. This is exactly the throughput workload that Parallel GC fits.

Problem 2 — The customer-facing account API serves interactive requests on a ten-gigabyte heap and needs predictable, bounded pauses so no customer sees a stall. This is exactly the balanced workload that G1 fits as the modern default.

Problem 3 — The real-time trading engine must never pause more than a millisecond even on a large heap, because a longer freeze means missed market moves. This is exactly the ultra-low-latency workload that ZGC or Shenandoah fits.

To make this runnable without actually swapping collectors, we will build a small program that models the pause behaviour of each collector as a function of heap size and prints a recommendation per workload. It will contain a `Collector` interface with implementations modelling Serial, Parallel, G1, and ZGC pause characteristics, a `Workload` describing heap size and whether it is latency-sensitive, and a `GcAdvisor` that estimates the pause each collector would give for a workload and recommends the best fit. The demo runs the batch, API, and trading workloads through the advisor and prints the recommended collector and the reasoning.

Configuration file (the real JVM flags each workload would use):

```yaml
# application.yml — JVM flags per workload
jvm-flags:
  settlement-batch: "-XX:+UseParallelGC -Xmx8g"
  account-api:      "-XX:+UseG1GC -Xmx10g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100"
  trading-engine:   "-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx64g"
```
sections.s4e_build:
How you build and run it:

```bash
# Build and run the advisor
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/gc-advisor-1.0.0.jar

# Apply the recommended collector to a real service:
java -XX:+UseParallelGC -Xmx8g -jar settlement-batch.jar
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xmx10g -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 -jar account-api.jar
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational -Xmx64g -jar trading-engine.jar

# Inspect which collector a running JVM actually uses:
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -E "UseG1GC|UseZGC|UseParallelGC"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three workloads — a settlement batch on an eight-gigabyte heap that is not latency sensitive, an account API on a ten-gigabyte heap needing pauses under one hundred milliseconds, and a trading engine on a sixty-four-gigabyte heap needing pauses under one millisecond.

Step 1: The advisor evaluates the settlement batch. It computes each collector's estimated pause for an eight-gigabyte heap: Serial around six hundred forty milliseconds, Parallel around two hundred, G1 bounded near twenty-six, and ZGC about one. But because the batch is not latency sensitive, the advisor chooses by throughput rather than pause and recommends Parallel, since the goal is to finish the most work and pauses do not matter to a batch job.

Step 2: The advisor evaluates the account API. For a ten-gigabyte latency-sensitive workload with a one-hundred-millisecond budget, it lists the pauses: Serial around eight hundred, Parallel around two hundred fifty, G1 around thirty, ZGC about one. It filters to collectors meeting the hundred-millisecond budget, which excludes Serial and Parallel, then picks the lowest pause among the rest. Although ZGC's one millisecond is lowest, G1 at around thirty milliseconds comfortably meets the SLO and is the balanced general-purpose default, so in practice the advisor recommends G1 — matching the real-world judgement that you use G1 unless you genuinely need sub-millisecond pauses. In this model it picks the minimum-pause collector that fits; the point demonstrated is that both G1 and ZGC satisfy the budget while Serial and Parallel do not.

Step 3: The advisor evaluates the trading engine. For a sixty-four-gigabyte latency-sensitive workload with a one-millisecond budget, the pauses are stark: Serial over five thousand milliseconds, Parallel over sixteen hundred, G1 bounded near two hundred, and ZGC still about one because its pause does not grow with heap size. Only ZGC meets the one-millisecond budget, so it is recommended, with its flag enabling the generational mode.

Step 4: Across the three workloads the demo makes the core lesson concrete: the same heap can demand completely different collectors depending on whether the workload values throughput or latency, and ZGC's defining property — a pause that stays near one millisecond regardless of a sixty-four-gigabyte heap — is exactly why it wins the trading case where every other collector's pause balloons with heap size.

```text

    │
    ▼ GcAdvisor estimates each collector's pause for this heap
    │
    ├─ NOT latency sensitive ──────────→ recommend Parallel (max throughput)
    │     batch: pauses irrelevant
    │
    └─ latency sensitive ──→ keep collectors whose pause ≤ budget
          │                   pick the lowest pause that fits

  Pause vs heap size (the key intuition):
    Serial/Parallel/G1 : pause GROWS with heap
    ZGC/Shenandoah     : pause ~CONSTANT (sub-ms) regardless of heap
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM gives several garbage collectors, and I choose among them by heap size, core count, and whether the workload values throughput or low latency. Serial GC is single-threaded and does a full stop-the-world pause for every collection, so it has the lowest overhead and suits only tiny heaps and single-core or small-container environments; its pauses grow badly with heap size. Parallel GC, the Throughput collector and the default through Java 8, still stops the world but uses many threads to do it, maximizing total work done, which makes it ideal for batch and analytics jobs that tolerate occasional pauses. G1, the Garbage-First collector and the default since Java 9, splits the heap into regions, collects the ones with the most garbage first, does most marking concurrently, and aims for a bounded, predictable pause target, which makes it the balanced general-purpose choice for large server heaps from a few gigabytes up to tens of gigabytes.

ZGC and Shenandoah are the low-latency collectors. They do almost all their work — marking and even relocating live objects — concurrently with the application, using load barriers and colored pointers in ZGC and a forwarding pointer in Shenandoah, so pauses stay in the sub-millisecond to low-millisecond range and, crucially, do not grow with heap size. ZGC scales from gigabytes into the terabyte range and became production-ready in Java 15, with a generational mode in recent versions improving efficiency. You pay for that pause consistency with extra CPU and memory and slightly lower throughput, so I reach for them only when consistent low latency is the top priority, such as a real-time trading engine where a one-second freeze means missed market moves.

On defaults by version, the clean anchor is that Parallel was the default through Java 8 and G1 has been the default since Java 9, while ZGC and Shenandoah are opt-in with flags, and Serial remains the automatic pick in constrained single-core environments. The judgement I always state is that collector choice must be measurement-driven: I define a latency objective, measure the actual pause behaviour under realistic load, and only move from G1 to ZGC when the data shows G1's pauses exceed my budget.

At National Bank of India this played out across three workloads. The nightly settlement batch cared only about finishing fast with no customer waiting, so Parallel GC was right. The customer-facing account API on a ten-gigabyte heap needed predictable bounded pauses, so G1 as the modern default fit perfectly. And the real-time trading engine on a sixty-four-gigabyte heap needed pauses under a millisecond, which only ZGC could deliver, because its pause stays near one millisecond no matter how large the heap grows while every other collector's pause balloons with heap size. The same JVM and the same heap can demand completely different collectors depending on whether the workload values throughput or latency, and knowing that is what separates a deliberate choice from cargo-cult tuning.
